title: First ASP.NET Core MVC Application
description: Create your first ASP.NET Core MVC application from scratch using Visual Studio 2022 or the dotnet CLI, add controllers, views, and models, and pass dynamic data to the browser.

data.text: In this lesson you will build your first ASP.NET Core MVC application from a blank project. You will create a controller with action methods, build Razor Views, pass data using both ViewBag and strongly-typed Models, and run everything in your browser.

data.title: Prerequisites
data.text: Make sure you have completed the previous lesson — the .NET 8.0 SDK and an editor (Visual Studio 2022 or VS Code) must be installed and working before you continue.
Create a New MVC Project
Open Visual Studio 2022 and select Create a new project under the Get Started section. In the template search box, type ASP.NET Core Web App (Model-View-Controller) and select it.

Name the project FirstApp, choose a location on your drive, and click Next. On the Additional Information page, confirm that .NET 8.0 is selected, Authentication is set to None, and Docker is unchecked. Click Create.
Alternatively, from the terminal you can create the same project with a single command:

data.title: Create an MVC Project with the CLI
data.content: Scaffold a new ASP.NET Core MVC project.
data.code:
dotnet new mvc -n FirstApp
cd FirstApp

data.text: Run the Application

Press F5 in Visual Studio, or run dotnet run from the terminal. Visual Studio opens your default browser and navigates to the home page. You should see the default ASP.NET Core welcome page with navigation links for Home, Privacy, and more.

data.title: Hot Reload
data.text: In Visual Studio 2022, Hot Reload lets you edit C# or Razor files while the app is running and see changes immediately without restarting. Look for the Hot Reload button in the toolbar.
MVC Files and Folders Explained
The template creates several folders and files automatically. Here is what each one does:

rows: Contains C# controller classes that handle incoming HTTP requests.
Contains C# classes that represent your application's data and business rules.
Contains Razor (.cshtml) templates that render HTML to the browser.
Contains static files — CSS, JavaScript, images, fonts, and vendor libraries like Bootstrap.
The application entry point. Configures services, middleware, and the web server.
Stores configuration such as connection strings and logging settings.
The project file. Lists dependencies, target framework, and build settings.

data.text: Adding a Controller
A Controller is a C# class whose job is to receive HTTP requests and return responses. Each public method in a controller is called an action method and can be invoked via a URL.

terms.definition: A C# class that inherits from Controller. It groups related action methods and sits between the browser and your data.
A public method inside a controller that handles a specific URL. Returns IActionResult.
The return type for action methods. It can represent a View, a redirect, a JSON response, a file, and more.

data.text: The default template already includes a HomeController. Let us add a new one called FirstController.

data.title: FirstController.cs
data.content: A new controller with an Index action that returns a plain text string.

data.text: Notice the file-scoped namespace declaration (namespace FirstApp.Controllers;) — this is a C# 10 feature that removes the extra wrapping braces and keeps code cleaner.
Run the app and navigate to /First/Index in the browser (replace the port with your own). You will see Hello World rendered directly — no View needed because the action returns a string.

data.title: Default Action Name
data.text: The Index action is the default. You can also navigate to /First without specifying the action name and it will still work.
Action Method Returning a View
Returning plain strings is useful for testing, but most real actions return Views — Razor HTML templates. Add a new action method called Hello that returns a View instead:

data.content: An action method that returns a View result.

data.text: Running /First/Hello at this point will throw an error — the runtime cannot find a View named Hello.cshtml. MVC looks for Views in two places: Views/First/Hello.cshtml (controller-specific) and Views/Shared/Hello.cshtml (shared across controllers).
Create the view by right-clicking the Views/First folder in Solution Explorer (or creating the folder manually) and adding a new Razor View called Hello.cshtml:

data.title: Views/First/Hello.cshtml
data.content: A simple Razor view that sets the page title and displays a heading.

data.text: Run the app and go to /First/Hello. You will see Hello World rendered in the browser with the page title set to Hello.
Passing Dynamic Data with ViewBag

ViewBag is a dynamic property bag attached to the View. Values you set in the Controller are automatically available in the View. It is great for passing simple values without creating a dedicated Model class.

data.title: Controller: Setting ViewBag.Message
data.content: Store a dynamic value in ViewBag from the controller.

data.title: View: Reading ViewBag.Message
data.content: Read the dynamic value from ViewBag inside the Razor view.

data.title: ViewBag vs ViewData
data.text: ViewBag is a dynamic wrapper around ViewData (a dictionary). ViewBag.Message and ViewData["Message"] access the exact same value. Use whichever syntax you prefer.
Passing a Strongly-Typed Model
ViewBag is flexible but gives no compile-time safety. For structured data, create a Model class and pass it to the View. This is the standard approach in production applications.

data.text: Use @model (lowercase) at the top of the view to declare the type. Use @Model (uppercase) inside the view to access the instance's properties.

Use the asp-action tag helper to generate links that point to controller action methods. Add a link on the Hello view that navigates to the Info view:

data.title: Exercise: Extend FirstController
data.description: Add two new features to the FirstController you just built.
steps: Add a Greet action method that accepts a string name parameter and returns Hello,  + name.
Navigate to /First/Greet/YourName and confirm the dynamic response.
Add a DisplayPerson action that accepts an int id parameter, looks up a Person in a hardcoded list, and passes it to a new DisplayPerson.cshtml view.
Create the DisplayPerson.cshtml view using a strongly-typed @model Person declaration and display all three properties.
data.expectedOutcome: You can navigate to /First/Greet/Alice and see a personalized response, and navigate to /First/DisplayPerson/1 to see a Person rendered from a Model.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Controllers are C# classes with action methods that map to URLs.
Action methods can return strings, View results, JSON, or redirects — always use IActionResult in production.
Views are Razor (.cshtml) files stored in Views/[ControllerName]/ or Views/Shared/.
ViewBag provides dynamic data passing with no compile-time safety.
Strongly-typed Models (via @model) give you IntelliSense and compile-time checking.
The asp-action tag helper generates correct links automatically.
data.takeaway: You have built your first functioning MVC app with controllers, views, and models. Next you will expand this knowledge into a full CRUD application with create, read, update, and delete operations.
